accuracy.evidence: Checked against Common Core RL.4.4 (words that allude to significant characters in mythology, e.g. Herculean), the National Curriculum in England reading programme (Years 3–6 myths and legends), and Merriam-Webster and the Online Etymology Dictionary: Herculean (Hercules/Heracles and the 12 labours, including the many-headed Hydra), Achilles' heel (Thetis dipping Achilles in the Styx, heel unprotected), Pandora's box (pithos/jar in Hesiod, box from Erasmus' later retelling), Midas touch (modern sense: ability to make money from anything), Trojan horse (Aeneid; also the computing sense), Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37), Scrooge (Dickens, A Christmas Carol, 1843), Waterloo (Napoleon's final defeat, 1815), panic (Greek panikos, of Pan), cereal (Latin Cerealis, of Ceres), volcano (Italian vulcano from Vulcanus), January (Latin Januarius, of Janus). The lesson notes that the Midas gift was a curse in the myth but is praise in modern use.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips with allusions: reading them literally (step 1 prediction Achilles' heel = sore foot, m3, challenge 'don't open the box', 'is about horses', 'a pan for cooking'), borrowing the wrong detail (step 3 options such as 'a very big animal', 'being a man', 'golden hands', p1 'done by a strong man', challenge Herculean 'very quick', Scrooge 'very old'), mixing up sources (Midas for a weak spot, Janus for panic), assuming a word has no story inside it (step 4 prediction on cereal), and skipping unknown names instead of looking them up (m7 Waterloo).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagallude taps the allusion chip inside a flowing sentence, drags allusion cards onto four myth summaries, asks which feature of a story (shown in a story card) the saying borrows with per-option feedback, drags everyday words (cereal, January, panic, volcano) onto Pan, Ceres, Vulcan and Janus, and reads Trojan horse, Good Samaritan, Midas and Achilles allusions in context. flagdevice (467, Figurative Language and Literary Devices) decodes three allusions in a mixed device lab and flagidiom matches idioms; neither traces myth words or borrowed features, and lab_distinct stayed under 30%.

lab_teaches.evidence: Feedback carries the teaching: tapping 'task.' says it is an ordinary word and to look for a name from a story; choosing 'a long war' for Trojan horse says 'The war is the background. The famous part is the trick'; putting cereal on Janus asks what cereal means and which god matches it; choosing 'a toy horse' says it reads the words literally and that the context shows harm hidden inside. Each correct move states the story link, e.g. 'Panic comes from Pan: a sudden fear like the one his shout caused'.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with a tempting wrong option: Achilles' heel means a sore foot (the spot and context steps show a weak spot), the Midas touch is a warning because Midas was cursed (the borrow step and the Ana sentence show modern praise for making money), and cereal is just a food word (the gods step traces it to Ceres).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six questions with tagged wrong options and messages naming the slip: literal reading ('reads the words literally; an allusion borrows the story's meaning, not the objects in it' for 'done by a strong man', 'don't open the box', 'haunted by ghosts', 'a pan for cooking' and 'is about horses'), the wrong part of the story ('very quick', 'very old', 'is very long': 'Ask what the story is famous for'), and the wrong source ('Midas touch', 'Herculean task', 'Janus, the god of doors': 'Match the name to its own story').

readability.evidence: validate_lessons passes the kid (≤ 6.5) and adult (≤ 9.5) limits. Kid paragraphs explain one idea each with one example (Herculean, Achilles' heel, Scrooge and panic) in short sentences, and the lab story cards are one-line summaries (did 12 labours that seemed impossible).

no_filler.evidence: No filler pattern matches. Every step has one job (spot, match, borrow, trace, read in context), and each item explanation gives the story fact and why the distractors fail, for example 'Pancake and pansy only share the letters p-a-n'.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 px (touch, 1.5x) in light and dark for every step before and after Show me: sentence chips wrap and centre, the four story or god boxes sit in a 2 by 2 grid, and the three meaning options stack full width. The god and story grid was moved up and shortened after the first screenshots showed a three-line feedback box covering the Vulcan and Janus boxes.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas move has a button: each word of the sentence ('Choose Herculean'), each story ('Pandora's box is from Pandora'), each borrowed feature, each god ('cereal comes from Ceres') and each meaning. The canvas aria-label reads the current sentence or card plus the last feedback, challenge feedback is an aria-live status, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
